title: Uncovering a pseudoscience: an analysis of 'biological dentistry' Instagram posts
screen_reason: Reports the share of items in a sample judged false/misleading against an external standard: 341 of 500 English-language 'Biological Dentistry' Instagram posts (68.2%) were coded as misinformation by two trained investigators. Denominator = all posts in the sampled corpus, so CONTENT.

estimates.country: Not stated (English-language posts; authors based in Brazil)
estimates.date: Posts published May 2017 to May 2022 (retrieved via CrowdTangle)
estimates.measure_type: % of 'Biological Dentistry' Instagram posts coded as containing misinformation
estimates.denominator: 500 English-language Instagram posts about 'Biological Dentistry', the 500 most-interacted posts of 3,775 retrieved by keyword/hashtag search on CrowdTangle for May 2017 - May 2022
estimates.definition: A post counted as misinformation if it 'propagated content that was demonstrably false or misleading, lacking a basis in scientific evidence'; the residual category ('Information') is reliable content. Coded from the post text, hashtags and images.
estimates.misinfo_def: "posts were identified as misinformation if they propagated content that was demonstrably false or misleading, lacking a basis in scientific evidence"; the study "employs 'misinformation' as an umbrella term" because author intent could not be established, so disinformation is not separated.
estimates.source_quote: Results: Over half of the posts (58.4%) were from health-related authors, and a considerable number contained misinformation (68.2%) or were financially motivated (52%).
estimates.page_loc: Results, p. 183; counts from Table 1 (Facticity: Information 159 (31.8%), Misinformation 341 (68.2%)), p. 186; also Abstract
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two trained, calibrated independent investigators (OSJ, YRM) coded every post; training on 10 posts with an experienced researcher, calibration on 10% of the sample (n = 50) with intraclass correlation coefficients from 0.778 (sentiment) to 0.937 (motivation), all above the 0.75 'good reliability' threshold; discrepancies resolved by discussion, with a third senior researcher (TC) deciding when consensus failed. Judgement is against scientific evidence, not against a fact-check database; the ICC for facticity specifically is not separately reported (only the range across the four coded variables).
estimates.moderator_quote: Initially, 3,775 'Biological Dentistry'-related posts published between May 2017 and May 2022 were retrieved from CrowdTangle, sorted by users' total interaction. Subsequently, two independent investigators (OSJ and YRM) qualitatively evaluated 500 of them using content analysis for the facticity, motivation, author's profile, and sentiment.
estimates.notes: IMPORTANT denominator caveat for pooling: the corpus is doubly selected. (a) The topic itself is a practice that Quackwatch classifies as dubious ('biological/holistic/functional dentistry'), and the search string is built from its promotional hashtags, so the denominator is a pseudoscience-topic corpus rather than a corpus of dental or health content in general - this figure is not the prevalence of misinformation in oral-health content on Instagram. (b) The 500 coded posts are the TOP 500 of 3,775 by total user interactions, i.e. rank-truncated on engagement, hence denom_selection=curated; the authors defend this as 'selectively focused on posts that demonstrated genuine user engagement'. Not within_misinfo_content, because the denominator is topic-defined rather than a misinformation-only sample. Year coded 2019 as the midpoint of the May 2017 - May 2022 publication window; the search itself was run in 2022. QUOTE NOTE: quote taken from the Abstract, which is the only place the 68.2% appears as a contiguous span in the text file (the Results paragraph is split across two interleaved columns). Table 1 gives the counts: 'Misinformation 341 (68.2%)'.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) NOT extracted (not misinformation shares): 58.4% of posts were by health-related authors (292/500), 52.0% were financially motivated (260/500), 59.8% conveyed negative or neutral sentiment (299/500) - these are author/motivation/sentiment composition, not veracity. They are, however, the paper's moderators of misinformation. 2) NOT extracted: odds ratios for misinformation (financial motivation OR = 2.12, 95% CI 1.40-3.21; health-related authorship OR = 5.56, 95% CI 3.67-8.44) and for overperforming score (non-health authorship OR = 1.98) - associations, not prevalence shares. 3) NOT extracted: interaction and overperforming-score medians by facticity (Table 1: misinformation median 893 total interactions vs information 884; overperforming 1.21 vs 1.51, P = 0.006) - engagement outcomes, not shares. 4) I did NOT create a subgroup row for misinformation by author type or by motivation: the cross-tabulated counts are not printed (only the marginal n(%) and the logistic-regression ORs), so no exact part/whole share is derivable. 5) The 3,775 posts retrieved is the full keyword corpus, but only the top 500 by interaction were coded, so no share can be computed on the 3,775 denominator. 6) Country: the study covers English-language posts worldwide with no country breakdown; the research team is Brazilian. Coded Global.

rob.design: Cross-sectional infodemiology content analysis of a rank-truncated platform corpus. Frame: CrowdTangle search of public Instagram posts using a 20-term keyword/hashtag string ('biological dentistry' OR #biologicaldentistry OR 'holistic dentistry' ... OR #integrativedentist) developed from a Google Ads KeywordPlanner exploratory analysis; 3,775 posts (May 2017 - May 2022) retrieved, filtered to English, sorted descending by total user interactions, and the top 500 manually reviewed for topical relevance, de-duplicated (including repost-app content), anonymised and fixed as a PDF so all coders saw identical content. No sampling probability, no response rate (non-human data; ethics approval not required for public internet data). Coding: two trained and calibrated independent investigators coded facticity, motivation, author profile and sentiment on all 500 posts; calibration on n = 50 with ICC 0.778-0.937; disagreements resolved by consensus, with a third senior researcher adjudicating. Analysis: Mann-Whitney U tests and multiple logistic regression (multicollinearity checked, VIF < 2.0), SPSS 28. Author-declared limitations: small hand-coded sample; no misinformation/disinformation distinction; English only; subjectivity of motivation and sentiment coding; no analysis of user comments; possible bot inflation of interaction metrics.
rob.item6_quote: Accordingly, posts were identified as misinformation if they propagated content that was demonstrably false or misleading, lacking a basis in scientific evidence [26, 31].
rob.item10_quote: The findings revealed that a majority of the posts contained misinformation (68.2%) and were driven by financial motives (52%).
